performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: Louis Frémaux conducts the Introït et Kyrie, the first movement of the Requiem, Op. 48. A single D sounds before the choir enters, and the movement is built from low strings, long-held chords and a tenor melody that returns as the Kyrie.

sections.label: A · A single D, then the choir
B · Tenor melody over strings and organ
sections.mNote: Tenor melody over violas, cellos, basses and organ.

sections.label: C · Winds before the soprano prayer
B′ · Kyrie for three voices
sections.mNote: The tenor melody returns in choral unison.

cues.title: Opening D and choral entry
cues.text: Bassoons, horns and low strings play D fortissimo, then fade. The choir enters pianissimo in six parts on a D minor chord. The violins and organ rest.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 1–4: opening D, six-part choir, and rests in the violin and organ parts. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/4c/IMSLP30151-PMLP21398-Faure-Op048fs.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Origins of the Requiem
cues.text: Fauré’s reasons for writing a Requiem are uncertain. His father died in 1885 and his mother on New Year’s Eve 1887, but he had begun the work before she died. In 1902 he wrote to Louis Aguettant that it was composed “for nothing … for pleasure, if I may say so”.
cues.evidence: Deaths of 1885 and 1887: Jeremy Summerly, Hyperion CDA68209 booklet note, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68209 . The work begun before the second death: Wadham Sutton, Hyperion note, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W4018_68209 (his mother died while it was in the early stages of composition); Jean-Michel Nectoux, Harmonia Mundi HMM 931292 booklet, https://www.harmoniamundi.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/931292_booklet.pdf (the work dates mainly from autumn 1887 and early 1888). Fauré to Louis Aguettant, 12 July 1902, published in Comœdia, 1954: “Mon Requiem a été composé pour rien… pour le plaisir si j’ose dire”, with the interview text at http://www.rene-gagnaux.ch/inghelbrecht_desire-emile/faure_requiem.html. Translation ours.

cues.title: First performance, the Madeleine, 1888
cues.text: The first performance was given at a funeral service at the Madeleine in Paris. On 16 January 1888 Fauré conducted five movements at the funeral of Joseph Lesoufaché, an architect. The Offertoire and the Libera me were added later.
cues.evidence: Date, occasion and five movements: Nectoux, Harmonia Mundi HMM 931292 booklet, https://www.harmoniamundi.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/931292_booklet.pdf (16 January 1888, the Madeleine, a funeral service, the composer conducting; the Offertoire and Libera me added later); Summerly, Hyperion CDA68209 booklet, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68209 (the funeral of Joseph Lesoufaché, an architect). The treble soloist of that service is not named here: Nectoux calls Louis Aubert the first Pie Jesu soloist without dating the service, and Aubert’s own sleeve account places his solo months after the première (see the Pie Jesu note).

cues.title: Andante moderato, tenor melody
cues.text: The marking changes to Andante moderato. Violas and cellos begin to move, and the tenors sing a falling melody over them. The organ enters on soft foundation stops while the horns and bassoons rest.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 5–9: Andante moderato, tenor melody and organ registration Fonds de 8 pieds.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wind chord before the sopranos
cues.text: Bassoons, horns and trumpets play a brief, strong chord before the soprano prayer. The organ adds reed stops, then returns to its foundation stops. The sopranos sing “Te decet hymnus” over moving violas and cellos.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 10–12: wind chords, organ registrations Anches et fonds and Fonds, and the soprano Te decet hymnus.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Exaudi”, full choir
cues.text: At “Exaudi” the whole choir sings fortissimo, and the next phrase is immediately softer. Fauré continues to alternate loud and soft phrases while the violas and cellos keep moving beneath the voices.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 13–15, rehearsal F: alternating ff and p in the choir and lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Kyrie, return of the tenor melody
cues.text: The Kyrie takes up the tenors’ earlier melody. Sopranos, altos and tenors sing it in unison before the writing divides into four parts. The bass line continues to move underneath.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 16–17: unison Kyrie followed by four-part writing; the melody recalls pp. 5–6.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “Christe”, choir and organ
cues.text: The first “Christe” is fortissimo, the next piano. The choir repeats this alternation above moving violas and cellos. The organ’s reed stops are added for the louder phrase.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 18–19: ff and p alternation, with Anches et fonds in the organ.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final Kyrie
cues.text: The choir returns to “Kyrie eleison” in short, quiet phrases. Cellos and basses continue beneath. Towards the end a bassoon and a horn play soft solo lines, and the movement closes on a chord of D minor.
cues.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 19–22: final Kyrie, dolce wind solos and D minor close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The priest at the Madeleine, 1888
cues.text: According to a story often retold, after the first performance at the Madeleine in January 1888 the priest called Fauré over and told him, “We have no need of all these novelties; the Madeleine’s repertoire is quite rich enough.”
cues.evidence: Retold in Jessica Duchen, Gabriel Fauré (Phaidon, 2000), p. 80 (as cited at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Requiem_(Faur%C3%A9); Duchen not opened); in Jeremy Summerly’s booklet note for Hyperion CDA68209, https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68209 (the priest-in-charge tells Fauré after the premiere that “we do not need these novelties”); in Lyle Chan’s ABC Classic guide, https://www.abc.net.au/listen/classic/read-and-watch/listening-guide/faure-requiem/11662990 (the Vicar calls Fauré over); and in French as “une petite histoire” on fr.wikipedia.org (“nous n’avons pas besoin de toutes ces nouveautés ; le répertoire de la Madeleine est bien assez riche”). All four are retellings and no first-hand account was found, so the note tells it as a story. The English is ours, from the French.

transitions.title: Fermata to the Andante moderato
transitions.from: A · A single D, then the choir
transitions.to: B · Tenor melody over strings and organ
transitions.how: A fermata holds the choir’s last chord. At the Andante moderato the tempo quickens and the D minor music continues with violas and cellos in flowing lines. The bass starts moving, and the organ enters on eight-foot foundation stops. The tenors take the melody alone, marked dolce espressivo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 4–5: fermata, new tempo, organ registration and tenor entry.

transitions.title: Wind chords before “Te decet hymnus”
transitions.from: B · Tenor melody over strings and organ
transitions.to: C · Winds before the soprano prayer
transitions.how: Bassoons, horns and trumpets return with strong chords over the low strings. The organ briefly adds reed stops, then goes back to its quieter foundation stops at rehearsal E. The strings make a diminuendo, and the sopranos enter with “Te decet hymnus”.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 10–11: wind chords, diminuendo, changes of organ registration and soprano prayer.

transitions.title: Full choir enters at rehearsal F
transitions.from: C · Winds before the soprano prayer
transitions.how: The strings crescendo beneath the end of the soprano prayer. At rehearsal F the full choir sings “Exaudi” fortissimo over a D minor chord. Violas, cellos and basses follow with forceful rising figures, and the next choral entry drops at once to piano.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 12–13: crescendo into rehearsal F and the alternating ff and p appeals.

transitions.title: Tenor melody returns as the Kyrie
transitions.how: The full choir makes a diminuendo at letter G and the wind chords fade. Sopranos, altos and tenors begin the Kyrie in unison on the earlier tenor melody, while the bass holds D beneath them. Violas and cellos resume their flowing accompaniment. The vocal marking is dolce espressivo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 15–16: diminuendo at G and unison Kyrie over the lower strings.

transitions.title: Kyrie into the first Christe
transitions.to: E · Christe eleison, loud and soft
transitions.how: A crescendo in the Kyrie leads to the first “Christe”, marked fortissimo. The organ adds reeds to its foundation stops (Anches et fonds), and the lower strings rise beneath the choir. A piano repetition follows at once, then a second fortissimo “Christe”, with the calls separated from one another.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 17–19: crescendo, Christe calls and Anches et fonds in the organ.

transitions.title: From the “Christe” into the final Kyrie
transitions.from: E · Christe eleison, loud and soft
transitions.how: The “Christe” calls diminish into the final Kyrie. The choir sings softly above moving cellos and basses, and the organ returns to foundation stops. The phrases in the lower strings continue up to the final D minor chord, marked pianissimo.
transitions.evidence: Hamelle full score (1901), pp. 19–22: final Kyrie and quiet D minor conclusion.

source.title: Fauré, Requiem, Op. 48, full orchestral score (Hamelle, 1901; Kalmus reprint)
source.locator: I. Introït et Kyrie, printed pp. 1–22: low strings, bassoons and horns at the opening; organ at the tenor prayer; trumpets in the later wind chords. The violins rest throughout.

timeline.note: Bassoons, horns and low strings play D. The six-part choir enters pianissimo; the organ is silent.
The tenors sing over low strings. The organ enters on its foundation stops.
Bassoons, horns and trumpets play forte chords, each marked to diminish.
The sopranos sing “Te decet hymnus” above violas and cellos. Bassoons and horns enter quietly at the end of the phrase.
The choir sings “exaudi” fortissimo. Strings play beneath soft wind chords.
The wind chords die away. The choir begins the Kyrie in unison, taking up the earlier tenor melody.
Voices, low strings and organ carry the Kyrie. The winds rest.
Pianissimo bassoon, horn and trumpet chords accompany the choir’s “Christe” calls.
The last Kyrie is pianissimo. Violas hold their notes while cellos and basses move beneath them.
A bassoon and horn add lines to the choir’s last phrases.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; neither has a solo part in this movement. The organist is named on the sleeve (“Chanoine Henri Carol”), not on Commons.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.

fields.note: Commons names “Erato Records” as source; the sleeve, BnF and Discogs give the Erato label.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The BnF notices list both issues with a 1962 legal-deposit date and cross-reference each other; the sleeve says the disc also exists in stereo as STE 50 128. Commons does not say which pressing, tape or CD its file derives from. The access MP3 is two-channel with a left/right correlation of 0.44 in this movement, so it is not a mono transfer, but that does not identify the carrier.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 1, track 1 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No transfer or restoration engineer is identified. Commons shows the file as uploaded by D. Benjamin Miller; an uploader is not assumed to be the engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+40 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.48 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Public domain in jurisdictions applying an unextended life-plus-70-year term
fields.note: Gabriel Fauré died in 1924. This assessment concerns the original composition, not a later edition, arrangement or this recording; it is not a worldwide rights clearance.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: Organist and teacher who wrote songs and chamber music in an unusual harmonic language.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; Saint-Saëns became his teacher and lifelong friend
Songs, piano music, chamber music, Requiem and the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
As a boy, Fauré often went into the chapel to play the harmonium. His father ran a teachers’ training school at Montgauzy, near Foix, and Gabriel Fauré’s first musical experiences were on the small instrument in its chapel. In October 1854 his father took him to Paris and enrolled him at Louis Niedermeyer’s new school for church musicians. He was nine. For eleven years he studied plainchant, the organ and the polyphony of Renaissance church music.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class. When the official lesson was over, he played the boys Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, composers well outside their syllabus. Saint-Saëns became Fauré’s teacher, champion and friend, and remained so for sixty years. Fauré left school in 1865 with prizes and the Cantique de Jean Racine, a setting of a French prayer over a flowing keyboard part, in which each new choral entry joins a phrase already under way.
